source_label: Jeukendrup 2011 A Step Towards Personalized Sports Nutrition
text: For marathon events lasting approximately 2–2.5 hours, carbohydrate ingestion of 30–60 g/hr during exercise is recommended to maintain blood glucose and spare muscle glycogen. Trained runners completing sub-3-hour marathons can typically absorb and oxidize up to 60 g/hr from a single carbohydrate source.

source_label: Pfeiffer et al. 2012 CHO Oxidation from Multiple Transportable CHO
text: For ultra-endurance events exceeding 2.5–3 hours (slow marathons, ultras), carbohydrate ingestion of 60–90 g/hr improves performance. To achieve oxidation rates above 60 g/hr without gut distress, multiple transportable carbohydrates (MTC) must be used — glucose and fructose together at approximately a 2:1 ratio — since intestinal transporters SGLT1 and GLUT5 are saturated at 60 g/hr when using glucose alone.

source_label: Jeukendrup 2011 A Step Towards Personalized Sports Nutrition
text: Carbohydrate ingestion during the marathon should begin early — within the first 30–45 minutes of racing — rather than waiting until the onset of fatigue. Early and consistent fueling maintains blood glucose and delays the onset of glycogen depletion. Many recreational runners make the mistake of waiting until they feel hungry or tired, which is too late to prevent the glycogen debt.

source_label: Jeukendrup 2011 A Step Towards Personalized Sports Nutrition
text: For practical race-day fueling with gels (typically 20–25 g CHO each), ingesting one gel every 20–30 minutes achieves 40–60 g CHO/hr. Elite runners consuming 90 g/hr will require larger servings or more frequent intake using MTC gels or chews. Gel intake should be paired with water (not sports drink) to manage osmolality and reduce gut distress risk.

source_label: Thomas Erdman Burke 2016 ACSM/AND/DC Position Nutrition and Athletic Performance
text: The pre-race meal should provide 1–4 g carbohydrate/kg body weight, consumed 1–4 hours before race start. Lower glycemic index foods consumed 3–4 hours prior are preferred; a smaller high-GI option 1–2 hours prior is acceptable for those with early start times. Avoid introducing unfamiliar foods on race day — practice pre-race meals during long training runs.

source_label: Pfeiffer et al. 2012 CHO Oxidation from Multiple Transportable CHO
text: The gastrointestinal (GI) tract can be trained to absorb higher carbohydrate amounts during running. Regularly consuming carbohydrates during long training runs (16+ km) upregulates intestinal SGLT1 transporter expression and increases CHO oxidation capacity. Runners targeting 60–90 g/hr race-day CHO should practice their fueling strategy in training, starting with lower amounts and progressively increasing.

source_label: Jeukendrup 2011 A Step Towards Personalized Sports Nutrition
text: Liquid carbohydrate sources (sports drinks, gels with water) empty from the stomach faster than solid foods and are preferred for faster marathon paces (above 5 min/km). At slower paces, solid foods (bananas, dates, rice cakes) are tolerated better and may improve palatability for long-distance events. Any solid food strategy should be practiced in training first.

source_label: Jeukendrup 2011 A Step Towards Personalized Sports Nutrition
text: In hot or humid conditions, GI motility is reduced due to splanchnic blood flow redirection. Runners should target the lower end of CHO intake ranges (30–45 g/hr) in temperatures exceeding 25°C, choose lower-osmolality beverages, and prioritize hydration over CHO density. High-carbohydrate gels in heat may increase nausea and vomiting risk.

source_label: Thomas Erdman Burke 2016 ACSM/AND/DC Position Nutrition and Athletic Performance
text: Caffeine is one of the most well-evidenced performance supplements for endurance running. Effective dose: 3–6 mg/kg body weight consumed 30–60 minutes before racing. Alternatively, mid-race caffeine (200–300 mg at km 25–30) may provide a second-half performance benefit and is particularly useful for runners who have already established a pre-race caffeine habit. Do not use caffeine for the first time on race day.

source_label: Thomas Erdman Burke 2016 ACSM/AND/DC Position Nutrition and Athletic Performance
text: Post-race nutrition should begin within 30–60 minutes of finishing. Target 1–1.2 g CHO/kg body weight plus 0.3–0.4 g protein/kg to initiate glycogen resynthesis and muscle protein repair. Early post-race nutrition is especially important if another performance is scheduled within 24–48 hours. Chocolate milk (4:1 CHO:protein ratio) is a practical and evidence-supported recovery option.

source_label: Jeukendrup 2011 A Step Towards Personalized Sports Nutrition
text: Individual carbohydrate absorption and tolerance vary substantially. Factors affecting race-day CHO oxidation include training status, gut microbiome composition, habitual dietary CHO intake, and prior gut training. Athletes should not attempt new gels or sports drinks on race day without prior testing. A conservative first-race strategy of 45 g/hr CHO and progression with experience is recommended.

source_label: Noakes 2012 Drink to Thirst During Exercise
text: At race aid stations, runners should consume fluids at every station in hot conditions, and every other station in cool conditions. The 2:1 glucose:fructose formula in sports drinks maximizes absorption. Mix commercial gels with water to reduce osmolality to approximately 270 mOsm/L. Avoid mixing gel with sports drink — combined hypertonicity worsens GI symptoms.

source_label: Noakes 2012 Drink to Thirst During Exercise
text: Current consensus strongly recommends drinking to thirst during marathon racing rather than following prescriptive scheduled drinking. The drink-to-thirst approach aligns fluid intake with individual sweat rates and prevents both dehydration and hyponatremia (overhydration). Runners with high-salt sweat (white residue on skin) should consume sodium-containing drinks rather than water alone.

source_label: Maughan Shirreffs 2012 Development of Hydration Strategies
text: Pre-race individual sweat rate assessment: Weigh yourself nude before and after a 1-hour training run at expected race pace and temperature without drinking. Sweat rate (L/hr) = (pre-weight – post-weight) + fluid consumed. This guides race-day fluid targets. Typical marathon runner sweat rates range 0.5–2.5 L/hr depending on body size and environment.

source_label: Casa et al. 2019 NATA Heat Illness Position Statement
text: Sodium intake during racing is critical for both fluid retention and preventing Exercise-Associated Hyponatremia (EAH). Sports drinks providing 500–700 mg sodium/L are recommended for events exceeding 2 hours. Sodium tablets (300–500 mg per tablet) can supplement electrolyte intake, particularly for slower runners spending 4+ hours on course in hot conditions where fluid intake is high.

source_label: Maughan Shirreffs 2012 Development of Hydration Strategies
text: Urine color is a practical hydration monitoring tool for pre-race and training contexts. Pale yellow (like lemonade) indicates adequate hydration. Dark amber indicates underhydration and performance may be impaired if >2% body weight is lost as fluid. Clear/colorless urine before a marathon may indicate overhydration — runners should not attempt to pre-hydrate to the point of clear urine.

source_label: Moran Wager 2019 Iron Status in Female Runners
text: Female endurance runners have substantially higher iron requirements than males due to menstrual blood loss, foot-strike hemolysis, and sweat losses. Recommended dietary intake for female runners is approximately 1.7× the general female population RDI. Ferritin levels below 30 ng/mL may impair aerobic performance even in the absence of clinical anemia. Female runners should monitor ferritin annually.

source_label: Moran Wager 2019 Iron Status in Female Runners
text: Dietary iron exists in two forms: heme iron (from red meat, poultry, fish) has 15–35% bioavailability; non-heme iron (legumes, fortified cereals, leafy greens) has 2–20% bioavailability. Consuming vitamin C-rich foods alongside non-heme iron sources enhances absorption. Avoid consuming iron-rich foods with coffee, tea, or calcium-rich foods, as polyphenols and calcium inhibit iron absorption.

source_label: Mountjoy et al. 2018 IOC Consensus RED-S
text: Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (RED-S) is common in female endurance runners and stems from Low Energy Availability (LEA): insufficient caloric intake relative to exercise energy expenditure. The minimum energy availability threshold is 45 kcal/kg lean body mass/day for healthy hormonal function. Warning signs include irregular or absent menstrual cycles, recurrent bone stress injuries, persistent fatigue, and mood disturbance.

source_label: Baar 2016 Nutrition and the Adaptation to Endurance Training
text: Nutritional needs vary across the menstrual cycle. In the luteal phase (days 15–28), basal metabolic rate increases by approximately 100–300 kcal/day, and carbohydrate oxidation during exercise is lower while fat oxidation is higher. Female runners may benefit from increased carbohydrate intake during the follicular phase and higher overall energy intake in the luteal phase to prevent LEA.

source_label: Thomas Erdman Burke 2016 ACSM/AND/DC Position Nutrition and Athletic Performance
text: Adequate calcium intake is essential for female runners to maintain bone mineral density and prevent stress fractures. Recommended intake: 1000–1300 mg/day. Vitamin D (1500–2000 IU/day in deficient athletes) is required for calcium absorption and bone metabolism. Female runners with stress fractures should be assessed for both calcium/vitamin D status and energy availability.

source_label: Thomas Erdman Burke 2016 ACSM/AND/DC Position Nutrition and Athletic Performance
text: Female endurance runners need 1.4–1.7 g protein/kg body weight/day to support muscle protein synthesis, bone remodeling, and immune function. Protein should be distributed across 3–4 meals of 20–30 g each to maximize muscle protein synthetic response. Post-run protein ingestion (20–25 g within 2 hours) is particularly important for recovery adaptations.

source_label: Moran Wager 2019 Iron Status in Female Runners
text: Iron status in female runners should be assessed using serum ferritin as the primary marker. Ferritin <30 ng/mL warrants dietary intervention; <15 ng/mL indicates iron deficiency and supplementation should be discussed with a sports medicine physician. Full blood count, transferrin saturation, and serum iron provide additional diagnostic information. Annual screening is recommended for all female runners in heavy training.

source_label: Mountjoy et al. 2018 IOC Consensus RED-S
text: Female runners are at elevated risk for disordered eating behaviors, particularly during pre-race weight management phases. Any restriction of intake below energy requirements, restriction of specific macronutrients, or distorted relationship with food and body weight warrants clinical assessment by a sports dietitian and physician. Coaches should not comment on athlete body weight or encourage restrictive eating.

source_label: Mountjoy et al. 2018 IOC Consensus RED-S
text: Nutritional needs increase substantially during pregnancy and postpartum recovery. Female runners returning to training postpartum should not reduce caloric intake to lose weight while breastfeeding, as LEA during lactation impairs milk production and maternal recovery. The minimum postpartum return-to-running energy availability threshold mirrors the non-pregnant athlete: ≥45 kcal/kg LBM/day.

source_label: Thomas Erdman Burke 2016 ACSM/AND/DC Position Nutrition and Athletic Performance
text: Vegan and vegetarian female runners face compounded nutritional risks: iron (non-heme only), vitamin B12 (absent in plant foods), calcium (if dairy-free), zinc, and omega-3 fatty acids. Iron absorption from plant sources is typically 5–15% bioavailable; dietary iron intake targets should be 1.8× higher for vegan athletes. Regular blood monitoring and targeted supplementation are advised.

source_label: Burke et al. 2011 Carbohydrates for Training and Competition
text: Carbohydrate loading (glycogen supercompensation) is the practice of maximizing liver and muscle glycogen stores before a marathon. Well-loaded muscles can store 500–800 g of glycogen (vs. 350–500 g baseline), representing an additional 8–14 minutes of race time at marathon pace. The benefit is most significant for runners targeting sub-3:30 finish times where glycogen depletion is a limiting factor.

source_label: Stellingwerff et al. 2019 Carbohydrate Loading Periodization
text: The classical 3-day carbohydrate loading protocol: Beginning 3 days before race day, increase CHO intake to 10–12 g/kg body weight/day while reducing training volume to near-zero. This protocol fully saturates muscle glycogen stores without requiring the preceding glycogen depletion phase used in older 7-day protocols. The key is achieving the CHO target across multiple small meals to avoid digestive overload.

source_label: Burke et al. 2011 Carbohydrates for Training and Competition
text: Practical food choices for carbohydrate loading at 10 g/kg (for a 65 kg runner = 650 g CHO/day): white rice (250 g dry ≈ 200 g CHO), pasta (200 g dry ≈ 150 g CHO), white bread (100 g ≈ 50 g CHO), bagels, crackers, sports drinks, gels, and fruit. During loading, avoid high-fiber foods (vegetables, legumes, whole grains) that can cause bloating and GI distress during the race.

source_label: Burke et al. 2011 Carbohydrates for Training and Competition
text: Many runners experience GI discomfort during carbohydrate loading due to increased water retention (glycogen stores ~3 g water per g glycogen) and large carbohydrate volume. Body weight may increase by 1–2 kg due to glycogen-bound water — this is normal and expected. To minimize bloating: eat frequently (5–6 small meals), choose low-fiber carbohydrates, reduce fat and protein, and avoid carbonated drinks.

source_label: Thomas Erdman Burke 2016 ACSM/AND/DC Position Nutrition and Athletic Performance
text: Race morning (3–4 hours before start): Consume a further 1–4 g CHO/kg body weight. Choose familiar, easy-to-digest options: oatmeal, toast, banana, sports drink. Avoid high-fat or high-protein foods that slow gastric emptying. Some runners prefer a liquid meal for faster digestion. Experiment with race-morning meals during long training runs to identify what works best individually.

source_label: Burke et al. 2011 Carbohydrates for Training and Competition
text: Elite runners (finishing under 2:30) benefit less from carbohydrate loading than recreational runners (3:30–5:00+) because elites may rely more on fat oxidation at race pace. Recreational runners completing marathons in 3.5–6 hours spend more time in glycogen-dependent pace zones and gain relatively more from complete glycogen loading. All runners completing more than 2.5 hours of racing should use a carbohydrate loading strategy.

source_label: Thomas Erdman Burke 2016 ACSM/AND/DC Position Nutrition and Athletic Performance
text: Caffeine is classified as an AIS Group A supplement (strong evidence of benefit) for endurance performance. Mechanism: reduces perception of effort (RPE) by adenosine receptor antagonism and may enhance fat oxidation. Effective dose: 3–6 mg/kg body weight. Response is individual — approximately 15–20% of athletes are non-responders due to genetic CYP1A2 variation. Side effects: anxiety, GI distress, insomnia (avoid within 8 hours of sleep).

source_label: Thomas Erdman Burke 2016 ACSM/AND/DC Position Nutrition and Athletic Performance
text: Dietary nitrate (from beetroot juice or greens) is an AIS Group A supplement shown to reduce oxygen cost of exercise by approximately 1–3%. Effective dose: 6–12 mmol nitrate (approximately 500 mL concentrated beetroot juice) daily for 3 days before competition, or a single acute dose 2–3 hours before. Most beneficial for recreational runners at slower speeds; effect diminishes in highly trained athletes.

source_label: Thomas Erdman Burke 2016 ACSM/AND/DC Position Nutrition and Athletic Performance
text: Creatine monohydrate has limited evidence for pure endurance (marathon) performance enhancement, as its primary mechanism (phosphocreatine resynthesis) is relevant only for high-intensity bursts. However, creatine may benefit marathon runners during heavy training phases by improving recovery between sessions and supporting high-intensity training intervals. Loading protocol: 20 g/day × 5 days, then 3–5 g/day maintenance.

source_label: Thomas Erdman Burke 2016 ACSM/AND/DC Position Nutrition and Athletic Performance
text: Protein supplementation (whey, casein, plant-based) is a practical strategy for runners struggling to meet daily protein targets through food alone. Whey protein post-exercise provides rapid leucine delivery optimal for muscle protein synthesis. Casein before sleep supports overnight muscle repair. Pea and rice protein combinations achieve comparable muscle protein synthesis to whey in controlled studies.

source_label: Thomas Erdman Burke 2016 ACSM/AND/DC Position Nutrition and Athletic Performance
text: Vitamin D deficiency is prevalent in runners training indoors or at northern latitudes. Serum 25-OH-D levels below 50 nmol/L (20 ng/mL) are associated with increased stress fracture risk and impaired immune function. Supplementation of 1000–2000 IU/day is commonly recommended to maintain adequate levels; higher doses (4000 IU/day) may be needed in documented deficiency. Test and treat, rather than blanket supplementing.

source_label: Thomas Erdman Burke 2016 ACSM/AND/DC Position Nutrition and Athletic Performance
text: Optimal racing weight is defined as the body composition at which an individual achieves peak performance, not the lowest achievable body weight. Running economy typically improves with lower body fat, but aggressive weight loss during training impairs recovery, hormonal function, and injury resistance. Pre-race weight loss attempts in the weeks before a marathon invariably reduce performance.

source_label: Mountjoy et al. 2018 IOC Consensus RED-S
text: Caloric restriction during heavy training phases (>10 hours/week) impairs adaptation, increases cortisol, reduces testosterone in male runners and disrupts menstrual function in female runners, and increases bone stress injury risk. Runners should not simultaneously pursue aggressive caloric restriction and high-training-load periods. Body composition changes occur more safely during reduced-load transition periods.

source_label: Thomas et al. 2016 ACSM/AND/DC Nutrition Position Stand
text: During heavy marathon training blocks (>80 km/week), daily carbohydrate needs are 6–10 g/kg body weight per day. This represents the primary fuel for high-volume endurance training. Inadequate CHO intake during training impairs session quality, accelerates glycogen depletion, and increases perceived exertion. Carbohydrate timing matters: prioritize intake around training sessions.

source_label: Burke et al. 2011 Carbohydrates Training Competition
text: During lower-intensity or reduced-load training weeks (40–60 km/week), daily CHO needs drop to 3–5 g/kg/day. This carbohydrate periodization approach — reducing CHO intake on light days and increasing on hard days — may enhance metabolic flexibility and promote greater fat oxidation capacity. This is distinct from chronic low-CHO training which impairs high-intensity adaptation.

source_label: Thomas et al. 2016 ACSM/AND/DC Nutrition Position Stand
text: Pre-training meal timing for marathon training: 3–4 hours before: full meal providing 2–3 g CHO/kg with moderate protein and low fat. 1–2 hours before: smaller snack of 1–2 g CHO/kg (banana, toast, sports gel). 30–60 minutes before: small easily digested CHO snack only if tolerated. Avoid high-fat or high-fiber foods within 2 hours of a quality training session.

source_label: Jeukendrup 2017 Training the Gut for Athletes
text: For training runs exceeding 75–90 minutes, carbohydrate supplementation during exercise (30–60 g/hr) maintains blood glucose and extends training quality. However, deliberately training without CHO intake in some easy sessions (fasted cardio, low sessions) may enhance mitochondrial adaptations. Rule: quality/intensity sessions are always fueled; some easy/aerobic sessions may be completed fasted.

source_label: Phillips & Van Loon 2011 Dietary Protein for Athletes
text: For marathon runners, total daily protein (1.4–1.7 g/kg/day) distributed across 4–6 equal portions of 20–30 g maximizes muscle protein synthesis. The most critical window is 30–120 minutes post-training: a meal or snack providing 20–30 g protein with leucine-containing foods (dairy, meat, eggs, legumes) initiates muscle repair. Protein before sleep (40 g casein) further supports overnight recovery.

source_label: Mountjoy et al. 2018 IOC Consensus RED-S
text: Maintaining adequate energy intake during high-mileage training is essential. Energy availability (EA) = dietary energy intake − exercise energy expenditure per kg lean body mass. Minimum EA: 45 kcal/kg LBM/day. Runners commonly under-fuel during high training loads due to appetite suppression post-exercise. Tracking food intake for 3–7 days every few weeks during training camps helps identify under-fueling.

source_label: Jeukendrup 2017 Training the Gut for Athletes
text: Marathon-specific long runs (>90 minutes) should be fueled with carbohydrates to simulate race conditions and train the gut. Begin CHO intake at 30–45 minutes into the run, consuming 30–60 g/hr from gels, sports drinks, or real food. Long runs completed without fueling deplete glycogen and compromise the training stimulus — this practice should be reserved for specific adaptation protocols under coaching guidance.

source_label: Thomas et al. 2016 ACSM/AND/DC Nutrition Position Stand
text: During long training runs, aim to begin drinking within 30 minutes of starting in warm conditions. A practical long-run hydration approach: carry a handheld water bottle or use aid stations/vending; supplement with electrolytes (salt tabs or electrolyte drink) for runs exceeding 2 hours. Weigh before and after to calculate sweat rate and dial in individual needs.

source_label: Jeukendrup 2011 Personalized Sports Nutrition
text: Some runners prefer real food during long runs (medjool dates, banana halves, rice cakes, energy chews). These are generally tolerated well at slower long-run paces. Real food provides additional micronutrients and has a lower glycemic index than gels. Test any new food during training runs only — never on race day. Foods should be easily portable and have a CHO density of ≥20 g per serving.

source_label: Ivy & Portman 2004 Nutrient Timing The Future of Sports Nutrition
text: Post-long-run nutrition window: consume 1–1.2 g CHO/kg + 0.3 g protein/kg within 30 minutes of finishing. This initial recovery window is critical — glycogen resynthesis rate is highest in the first 30–60 minutes post-exercise. Subsequent meals should continue to provide CHO and protein. A whole-milk recovery shake, rice with chicken, or yogurt with fruit/granola are practical options.

source_label: Thomas et al. 2016 ACSM/AND/DC Nutrition Position Stand
text: Sleep is the primary recovery modality for marathon runners; nutrition around sleep supports hormonal recovery. Growth hormone release peaks in the first 90 minutes of sleep — adequate caloric intake (not caloric deficit) during the pre-sleep window maximizes this anabolic response. Avoid heavy exercise or large caloric restriction in the 3–4 hours before sleep during heavy training periods.

source_label: Thomas et al. 2016 ACSM/AND/DC Nutrition Position Stand
text: Omega-3 fatty acids (EPA/DHA) have anti-inflammatory properties relevant to marathon training recovery. Supplementation with 2–4 g EPA+DHA daily may reduce delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS) and training-associated inflammation. Food sources: fatty fish (salmon, mackerel, sardines) ≥2×/week. For runners following plant-based diets, algae-based DHA/EPA supplements are the preferred source.

source_label: Thomas et al. 2016 ACSM/AND/DC Nutrition Position Stand
text: Tart cherry juice is an evidence-supported recovery aid, particularly for reducing muscle damage markers and DOMS after long runs and races. Protocol: 500 mL tart cherry juice (or equivalent concentrate) twice daily for 4–5 days before and 2–3 days after a major race or long training run. Contains anthocyanins and melatonin. Not AIS Group A (evidence is encouraging but moderate).

source_label: Thomas et al. 2016 ACSM/AND/DC Nutrition Position Stand
text: Vitamin C-enriched gelatin (or hydrolyzed collagen) taken 30–60 minutes before exercise or physical therapy may enhance collagen synthesis in tendons, ligaments, and cartilage. Protocol: 15 g gelatin/hydrolyzed collagen + 50 mg vitamin C, 30–60 minutes before training. Most evidence is from tendon-specific studies; application to marathon runners managing Achilles or plantar issues is emerging.

source_label: Phillips & Van Loon 2011 Dietary Protein for Athletes
text: Plant-based marathon runners must ensure complete protein intake. While individual plant proteins are often limiting in specific amino acids, combining complementary sources throughout the day achieves complete amino acid profiles: legumes + grains, tofu/tempeh + rice, quinoa (complete protein on its own). Leucine content of plant proteins is generally lower than animal sources — plant-based runners may need 20–30% higher total protein intake.

source_label: Thomas et al. 2016 ACSM/AND/DC Nutrition Position Stand
text: Gluten-free diet is medically indicated for runners with celiac disease or non-celiac gluten sensitivity. Without these diagnoses, a gluten-free diet does not improve performance or GI symptoms in runners. Gluten-free carbohydrate sources: rice, quinoa, oats (certified GF), potatoes, sweet potatoes. Avoid over-relying on commercial GF products high in refined starch and low in fiber or micronutrients.

source_ref: Thomas et al. 2016 Eur J Sport Sci; Lis et al. 2019 Nutrients
text: Low-FODMAP protocol for GI-sensitive runners: Gastrointestinal (GI) distress affects 30–65% of marathon runners, impairing performance and quality of life. For runners with functional GI symptoms (bloating, cramping, diarrhea during training), a supervised low-FODMAP (Fermentable Oligo-, Di-, Mono-saccharides And Polyols) elimination phase (2–6 weeks) can identify dietary triggers. Common high-FODMAP culprits in sports nutrition: lactose-containing gels, fructose-heavy energy chews, apple/pear-based products, wheat-based bars. Low-FODMAP race day alternatives: glucose-based gels, rice-based products, banana, white bread with honey. Reintroduction phase (weeks 3–8) is essential to restore dietary diversity. Critical: the low-FODMAP protocol is not a long-term diet and significantly restricts prebiotic fibre critical for gut microbiome health. Implementation requires guidance from a sports dietitian experienced in endurance athletes to avoid nutritional deficiencies, particularly calcium and prebiotic fibre. Do not self-prescribe long-term FODMAP restriction without professional supervision.
